proof:
Use 5f266955bbf5ddab for the actual maximum over the three interval fibers with arbitrary positive probabilities $p_-,p_0,p_+$. Its three values are $p_-/2$, $p_0/2+\min(p_-,p_+)$ and $p_+/2$, with unique endpoint maximizers at their midpoints. The middle midpoint is also its fiber's unique maximizer: at height $x$, choose the continuous orientation selecting the shorter own interval trace, and add a sufficiently large signed base tilt through $(0,x)$ to capture all of the lighter endpoint and none of the other endpoint. This bounds depth by $p_0(1-|x|)/2+\min(p_-,p_+)$, strictly below the middle maximum when $x\ne0$. The accepted formula includes every closed ambient halfspace. At the original uniform weights it gives the stated depths $1/2$ and $1/6$.

The reflected Gaussian weights are proportional to $(b/r,1,br)$, since the tilt at each base $z$ is $e^{az-tz^2/2}$. Comparing the heavier endpoint with the middle gives exactly the stated branch inequality. The lighter endpoint is strictly below the middle value. An endpoint winner or tie requires $br\ge1+2b/r>1$, so the ratio of largest to smallest likelihood ratio is then $R=r^2$, because the prior is uniform. The inequality $br\ge1+2b/r$ is equivalent to $b(r^2-2)\ge r$. For $b\le1$ and $r\ge1$, this requires $r\ge2$, with equality possible only for $b=1$. Strict inequality requires $r>2$. For any $R>4$, take $r=\sqrt R$ and choose $r/(r^2-2)<b<1$, giving a strict endpoint winner at positive time. Alternatively take $r=1$ and $b=1/R$, which gives the same oscillation and the unique middle winner.

Apply pk-w34-payments-sharp-posterior-event-correction with the uniform prior on three fibers. The envelope is strictly increasing, and its first segment ends at posterior mass $p_{\max}$ and original mass $1/3$. Thus a posterior depth $D_*$ corrects to at least $1/4$ precisely when $D_*\ge(3/4)p_{\max}$. No endpoint branch can satisfy this because its maximum is at most $p_{\max}/2$. For the middle value the condition becomes $2+4b/r\ge3\max\{1,br\}$. Its two simultaneous inequalities give $r\le4b$ and $3br^2-2r-4b\le0$. Solving the latter gives the stated second upper bound on $r$, and $r\ge1$ forces $b\ge1/4$. These conditions themselves force a strict middle winner.

At $(b,r)=(1/2,2)$ the posterior weights are $(1,4,4)/9$, and the actual maximum $1/3$ lies in the first segment and corrects to $1/4$. At $(1/2,8)$ the posterior weights are $(1,16,64)/81$, and the actual maximum $32/81$ at $(1,0)$ corrects to $1/6$. An actual cap through that endpoint midpoint that takes precisely half of its interval and excludes both other fibers realizes equality. Finally, if $r=1$, the middle always wins with posterior maximum $1/2$. For $b\le1/2$ this is in the first segment because $p_0=1/(1+2b)\ge1/2$, giving corrected value $(1+2b)/6$. The same mark's original depth is $1/2$ throughout.
statement:
Use the actual three-interval product with bases $-1,0,1$, identical intervals $[-1,1]$, and uniform original base probabilities. After possibly reflecting the base, a Gaussian posterior has weights proportional to $(b/r,1,br)$ with $b=e^{-t/2}\in(0,1]$ and $r=e^{|a|}\ge1$. Its deepest mark is the middle midpoint if $br<1+2b/r$, the positive endpoint midpoint if $br>1+2b/r$, and exactly those two at equality. Their original depths are $1/2$ and $1/6$. If $R$ is the ratio of the largest to the smallest likelihood ratio, a strict endpoint winner occurs only for $R>4$, and every $R>4$ allows a strict endpoint winner at positive time and a separate posterior with the middle winner. A tie with the endpoint at $R=4$ requires $t=0$.

The scalar correction of the exact posterior maximum meets the target $1/4$ precisely when
$$
b\ge1/4,\qquad 1\le r\le\min\{4b,\,(1+\sqrt{1+12b^2})/(3b)\}.
$$
For $(b,r)=(1/2,2)$ the corrected value is $1/4$. For $(b,r)=(1/2,8)$ it is $1/6$, attained by an actual isolated endpoint cap. Along $r=1,\ b\le1/2$ it is $(1+2b)/6$, though the actual original depth of the winning mark remains $1/2$.
title: Exact posterior selection and correction thresholds for three equal intervals
